CPU Scheduling Analysis: Non-Preemptive SJF vs Preemptive SRTF

CPU scheduling algorithms are fundamental operating system mechanisms designed to maximize CPU utilization and minimize process wait and turnaround times. Shortest Job First (SJF) selects the process with the smallest burst time from the ready queue. In its non-preemptive variant, once a process is allocated the CPU, it runs to completion. In contrast, Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) is the preemptive version of SJF, where the currently executing process is preempted if a newly arrived process (or a process in the ready queue) possesses a strictly shorter remaining burst time.

Dining Philosophers Synchronization Solution using Monitors

The Dining Philosophers Problem is a classic concurrency synchronization problem illustrating the challenges of allocating shared resources among multiple processes without causing deadlocks or starvation. Five philosophers sit around a circular table with five chopsticks. A philosopher requires two adjacent chopsticks to eat. Using lower-level synchronization primitives like raw semaphores can easily result in a deadlock if every philosopher simultaneously picks up their left chopstick. To guarantee deadlock-free execution, a high-level synchronization construct known as a Monitor is utilized.

A Monitor encapsulates private state variables, condition variables, and public procedures into an abstract data type where only one thread can execute inside the monitor at any given time. In the Dining Philosophers solution, chopsticks are not tracked as individual explicit objects; instead, the state of each philosopher is maintained explicitly as THINKING, HUNGRY, or EATING. A philosopher is allowed to transition to EATING only if neither of their immediate neighbors is currently eating.

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> THINKING THINKING --> HUNGRY : pickup() called HUNGRY --> EATING : test() succeeds (neighbors not eating) HUNGRY --> HUNGRY : wait on condition variable EATING --> THINKING : putdown() called & test neighbors

Monitor Implementation Code (Preventing Deadlocks)

Below is the complete pseudocode implementation of the DiningPhilosophers monitor, employing condition variables self[5] to block hungry philosophers until both chopsticks become available simultaneously.


monitor DiningPhilosophers {
    enum { THINKING, HUNGRY, EATING } state[5];
    condition self[5];

    procedure pickup(int i) {
        state[i] = HUNGRY;
        test(i);
        if (state[i] != EATING) {
            self[i].wait(); // Block until signaled by a neighbor
        }
    }

    procedure putdown(int i) {
        state[i] = THINKING;
        // Test left neighbor ((i + 4) % 5) and right neighbor ((i + 1) % 5)
        test((i + 4) % 5);
        test((i + 1) % 5);
    }

    procedure test(int i) {
        if ((state[(i + 4) % 5] != EATING) &&
            (state[i] == HUNGRY) &&
            (state[(i + 1) % 5] != EATING)) {
            
            state[i] = EATING;
            self[i].signal(); // Resume philosopher if waiting
        }
    }

    initialization_code() {
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            state[i] = THINKING;
        }
    }
}

Deadlock & Starvation Analysis

  • Deadlock Freedom: Deadlock is strictly prevented because state transitions and chopstick allocations occur atomically within monitor procedures. A philosopher transitions to EATING only when both adjacent chopsticks are confirmed free via the test() procedure. A philosopher never holds one chopstick while waiting indefinitely for the second.
  • Starvation Consideration: While this monitor structure is immune to deadlock, a philosopher could theoretically suffer from starvation if their left and right neighbors alternate eating indefinitely. Fair queueing extensions or aging mechanisms can be added to guarantee bounded waiting.

Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol and its Variants

The Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is a concurrency control mechanism widely employed in database management systems and transactional operating systems to guarantee serializability. Serializability ensures that concurrent execution of transactions yields the exact same outcome as executing them in some sequential order. 2PL achieves this by requiring each transaction to acquire and release locks in two distinct, non-overlapping phases during its lifecycle.

1. Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Mechanics

The execution of a transaction under standard 2PL is strictly partitioned into two phases:

  • Growing Phase (Lock Acquisition): The transaction may acquire new locks (Shared \(S\) locks for reading or Exclusive \(X\) locks for writing) as needed. It cannot release any locks during this phase.
  • Lock Point: The exact instant when the transaction acquires its final required lock, marking the end of the growing phase.
  • Shrinking Phase (Lock Release): The transaction begins releasing locks. Once the first lock is released, the transaction enters the shrinking phase and is strictly forbidden from acquiring any new locks.
graph LR A[Transaction Starts] --> B[Growing Phase: Acquire S/X Locks] B --> C[Lock Point: Max Locks Held] C --> D[Shrinking Phase: Release Locks] D --> E[Transaction End / Commit]

2. Strict 2PL vs. Rigorous 2PL

While basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability, it is susceptible to cascading rollbacks (where the abort of one transaction forces the abort of multiple dependent transactions that read uncommitted data). To prevent cascading aborts and ensure recoverability, enhanced variants of 2PL are used:

Feature Basic 2PL Strict 2PL Rigorous 2PL
Exclusive Lock Release Released during shrinking phase before commit. Held strictly until transaction commits or aborts. Held strictly until transaction commits or aborts.
Shared Lock Release Released during shrinking phase before commit. Released gradually during shrinking phase. Held strictly until transaction commits or aborts.
Cascading Aborts Possible (allows dirty reads of uncommitted data). Prevented (No dirty reads allowed). Prevented (No dirty reads allowed).
Concurrency Level Highest concurrency among 2PL variants. Moderate concurrency. Lowest concurrency (strictest locking).
Serialization Order Determined by Lock Point. Determined by Lock Point / Commit order. Determined strictly by transaction Commit order.

Detailed Analysis of Variants:
In Strict 2PL, holding all Exclusive (\(X\)) locks until transaction commit guarantees that uncommitted data written by a transaction cannot be read or modified by any other transaction, thereby eliminating dirty reads and enforcing strict recoverability. In Rigorous 2PL, the requirement is extended to all locks (both Shared \(S\) and Exclusive \(X\)). Consequently, lock release coincides entirely with the commit operation, completely eliminating the shrinking phase before commit. This simplifies transaction recovery and logging at the cost of reduced concurrency.

Swap Space Management in Linux/UNIX Systems

Swap Space is a designated region of secondary storage (hard disk drive or solid-state drive) utilized by the operating system as an extension of physical RAM. When main memory becomes constrained, the kernel page-out mechanism moves inactive or idle memory pages from RAM to swap space. When a process subsequently accesses a swapped-out page, a page fault occurs, causing the kernel to bring the page back into RAM (page-in operation). Efficient swap space management is essential for operating system stability, preventing Out-Of-Memory (OOM) process terminations.

In Linux/UNIX systems, the kernel tracks swap space using data structures like swap_info_struct and a Swap Map array, where each entry represents a page-sized slot in the swap area. Linux also implements a Swap Cache to synchronize shared pages and prevent duplicate block writes to disk.

graph TD UserApp[User Memory Page Requests] --> VirtualMemory[Virtual Memory Manager / MMU] VirtualMemory -->|RAM Available| PhysicalRAM[Physical RAM Memory] VirtualMemory -->|RAM Exhausted| SwapSubsystem[Linux Swap Subsystem] SwapSubsystem -->|Raw Access| SwapPartition[Raw Swap Partition /dev/sda2] SwapSubsystem -->|VFS Path| SwapFile[Swap File /swapfile via Filesystem]

Swap Raw Partition vs. Swap File Implementation

Linux supports two primary methods for backing swap space: dedicated Swap Raw Partitions and filesystem-based Swap Files.

Dimension Raw Swap Partition Swap File
Storage Structure Dedicated unformatted disk partition (e.g., /dev/sda2). Regular pre-allocated file inside an existing filesystem (e.g., /swapfile).
I/O Overhead & Performance Bypasses Virtual File System (VFS) and filesystem metadata structures. Writes directly to disk blocks, offering maximum I/O speed. Incurs slight VFS and filesystem mapping overhead (lookup of extent block locations), though modern kernels bypass caching layers.
Flexibility & Resizing Inflexible. Resizing requires disk repartitioning (modifying partition tables using fdisk/gparted) or LVM reconfiguration. Highly flexible. Can be dynamically created, expanded, or deleted using standard utilities (fallocate, mkswap, swapon).
File Fragmentation Zero file fragmentation since block allocation is contiguous across the partition. Potential fragmentation if created on a fragmented filesystem, which can impair sequential swap throughput.

Implementation Workflow:
To initialize a swap file in Linux, an administrator executes: fallocate -l 4G /swapfile, sets strict permissions chmod 600 /swapfile, formats it with mkswap /swapfile, and activates it via swapon /swapfile. Modern Linux kernels (version 2.6+) format swap files by mapping out physical extent block numbers directly, making swap file performance virtually identical to raw partitions.

Memory Fragmentation and Compaction Algorithms

Memory management subsystems must dynamically allocate and deallocate memory blocks to running processes. Over time, these allocations give rise to Memory Fragmentation, which degrades memory utilization and system performance. Fragmentation occurs in two distinct forms:

  • Internal Fragmentation: Occurs when memory is allocated in fixed-size blocks or units (e.g., page frames or power-of-two blocks). If a process requests less memory than the allocated block size, the remaining unused space inside the block is wasted and cannot be assigned to other processes.
  • External Fragmentation: Occurs when total free physical memory is sufficient to satisfy a process allocation request, but the free space is broken up into numerous small non-contiguous holes. As a result, no single contiguous free block is large enough to fulfill the request.

Memory Compaction Mechanics

Compaction is a technique used to resolve external fragmentation in dynamic memory allocation systems. It involves shifting allocated processes in physical memory so that all occupied blocks are moved to one end, coalescing all fragmented free spaces into a single, large contiguous block of memory.

Requirement: Compaction is feasible only if the system supports dynamic relocation at execution time, where address translation is performed dynamically via CPU relocation/base and limit registers.

graph TB subgraph Before Compaction B1["P1 (100 KB) @ 0"] --- B2["Free (50 KB)"] --- B3["P2 (150 KB) @ 150"] --- B4["Free (100 KB)"] --- B5["P3 (80 KB) @ 400"] --- B6["Free (20 KB)"] end subgraph After Compaction A1["P1 (100 KB) @ 0"] --- A2["P2 (150 KB) @ 100"] --- A3["P3 (80 KB) @ 250"] --- A4["Contiguous Free Space (170 KB) @ 330"] end

Execution Trace of Memory Compaction

Consider a physical memory space of \(500\text{ KB}\) with the following initial fragmented state:

Memory Region Start Address End Address Size Status
Block 10 KB100 KB100 KBAllocated to Process P1
Hole 1100 KB150 KB50 KBFree Space
Block 2150 KB300 KB150 KBAllocated to Process P2
Hole 2300 KB400 KB100 KBFree Space
Block 3400 KB480 KB80 KBAllocated to Process P3
Hole 3480 KB500 KB20 KBFree Space

Total Free Space before compaction: \(50\text{ KB} + 100\text{ KB} + 20\text{ KB} = 170\text{ KB}\).
If a new process P4 requests a contiguous block of \(140\text{ KB}\), the allocation fails under standard dynamic allocation (First-Fit / Best-Fit) despite having \(170\text{ KB}\) total free space due to external fragmentation.

Compaction Execution Steps:

  1. Process P1 remains at base address \(0\text{ KB}\).
  2. Process P2 is relocated downwards by \(50\text{ KB}\). Its new base register value changes from \(150\text{ KB}\) to \(100\text{ KB}\) (occupying range \(100\text{ KB} - 250\text{ KB}\)).
  3. Process P3 is relocated downwards by \(150\text{ KB}\). Its new base register value changes from \(400\text{ KB}\) to \(250\text{ KB}\) (occupying range \(250\text{ KB} - 330\text{ KB}\)).
  4. All free holes are merged into a single contiguous free block spanning \(330\text{ KB} - 500\text{ KB}\) (total size \(170\text{ KB}\)).
  5. The request for P4 (\(140\text{ KB}\)) can now be successfully allocated from \(330\text{ KB}\) to \(470\text{ KB}\).

System Call Implementation via Interrupt Vectors and Software Traps

A System Call provides the essential interface between a user-space application and the privileged operating system kernel. User applications execute in unprivileged User Mode (Ring 3), which prevents direct access to system hardware, memory control registers, and privileged instructions. To access system resources (e.g., file I/O, process creation, network sockets), the application must request kernel execution in Kernel Mode (Ring 0) via a system call mechanism.

1. Software Traps and Interrupt Vector Control Flow

The invocation and hardware execution of a system call follow a strictly defined sequence:

  1. System Call Setup: The user application loads the unique system call identity number into a specified CPU register (e.g., EAX/RAX on x86, x8 on ARM64) and places arguments into designation registers or stack locations.
  2. Software Trap Execution: The application executes an explicit trap instruction (e.g., int 0x80, syscall, or sysenter). This hardware instruction raises a controlled software exception.
  3. Privilege Level Switch & Trap Table Lookup: The hardware automatically transitions the CPU execution mode from User Mode (Ring 3) to Kernel Mode (Ring 0). The CPU indexes the Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT) or Interrupt Vector Table using the trap vector to locate the registered kernel entry point address.
  4. State Preservation & Kernel Handler Execution: The kernel pushes user register states onto the process's kernel stack. The kernel dispatch table (e.g., sys_call_table) maps the call number to the target kernel function (e.g., sys_read()) and executes it.
  5. Return to User Space: Upon completion, the result is saved in a return register (e.g., RAX), user state is restored, and a specialized instruction (sysret or iret) switches execution back to Ring 3.
sequenceDiagram participant UserApp as User Program (Ring 3) participant CPU as CPU Hardware participant IDT as Interrupt Vector Table / IDT participant Kernel as Kernel Handler (Ring 0) UserApp->>CPU: Load Syscall Number & execute 'syscall' / 'int 0x80' CPU->>CPU: Switch to Ring 0 & Save Stack Context CPU->>IDT: Lookup Vector Entry Point IDT->>Kernel: Jump to System Call Dispatcher Kernel->>Kernel: Save Registers & Execute sys_xxx() Kernel->>CPU: Return Result in RAX & Execute 'sysret' CPU->>UserApp: Restore Ring 3 & Resume Execution

2. System Call Parameter Passing Methods

Operating systems employ three fundamental techniques for passing parameters from user space to the kernel during a system call:

  • CPU Registers (Fastest): Parameters are loaded directly into designated hardware registers prior to issuing the trap.
    Example (Linux x86_64 ABI): Arguments are passed in RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8, and R9.
    Trade-off: High performance due to zero memory access overhead, but limited by the fixed number of CPU registers available.
  • Memory Block / Parameter Table: When parameters exceed available registers, they are stored in a contiguous block in user memory space. A single pointer to the memory block address is passed to the kernel via a CPU register.
    Trade-off: Supports arbitrary numbers and sizes of arguments, but requires the kernel to perform explicit safety validation and memory copies (e.g., copy_from_user()).
  • User Stack: Parameters are pushed onto the user application stack by the program and popped off by the kernel trap handler.
    Trade-off: Flexible and traditional, but requires kernel inspection of user stack pointers.

File Locking Mechanisms and `fcntl()` Implementation

In multi-process operating systems, multiple processes may attempt to read or write to the same file concurrently. Without proper synchronization, concurrent writes can lead to file corruption and data races. File Locking provides concurrency control mechanisms to regulate file access across independent processes.

1. Classification of File Locks

File locking mechanisms are classified according to lock modes and kernel enforcement policies:

  • Shared Lock (Read Lock, F_RDLCK): Multiple processes can simultaneously hold shared locks on the same byte range of a file. Shared locks allow concurrent reading, but prevent any process from acquiring an exclusive write lock.
  • Exclusive Lock (Write Lock, F_WRLCK): Only a single process can hold an exclusive lock on a file region at any time. It guarantees exclusive write access, denying both shared read locks and exclusive write locks to all other processes.
  • Advisory Locking: The default file locking mode in Linux/UNIX. Advisory locks are not enforced automatically by standard system calls like read() or write(). Cooperating processes must explicitly inspect and request locks using API calls (e.g., fcntl()). Non-cooperating processes that bypass lock checks can still perform direct I/O.
  • Mandatory Locking: Mandatory locks are enforced directly by the kernel on every read() and write() system call. If a file region is exclusively locked, attempts by any process to write to or read from that region are blocked or rejected by the OS, regardless of whether the process called locking APIs.

2. Complete C Code Implementation using `fcntl()`

The fcntl() system call provides POSIX-compliant record/byte-range locking. Below is a complete C program demonstrating how to acquire an exclusive lock on a file, perform write operations, and unlock the file safely.


#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <errno.h>

int main() {
    int fd;
    struct flock fl;
    const char *text = "Critical file record entry written by Process PID: ";
    char buffer[128];

    // Open file for reading and writing
    fd = open("system_log.txt", O_RDWR | O_CREAT, 0666);
    if (fd == -1) {
        perror("Error opening file");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    // Configure flock structure for an Exclusive Write Lock
    memset(&fl, 0, sizeof(fl));
    fl.l_type   = F_WRLCK;    // Exclusive write lock
    fl.l_whence = SEEK_SET;   // Offset relative to beginning of file
    fl.l_start  = 0;          // Lock starting offset
    fl.l_len    = 0;          // 0 means lock to end-of-file (entire file)
    fl.l_pid    = getpid();

    printf("Process %d: Attempting to acquire Exclusive Write Lock...\n", getpid());

    // Acquire lock (F_SETLKW blocks until lock is granted)
    if (fcntl(fd, F_SETLKW, &fl) == -1) {
        perror("fcntl acquire lock failed");
        close(fd);
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }

    printf("Process %d: Lock acquired successfully. Writing data...\n", getpid());

    // Perform Critical Section Write Operations
    snprintf(buffer, sizeof(buffer), "%s%d\n", text, getpid());
    lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END);
    write(fd, buffer, strlen(buffer));
    sleep(3); // Simulate file processing time

    // Release the Lock
    fl.l_type = F_UNLCK; // Change lock type to unlock
    if (fcntl(fd, F_SETLK, &fl) == -1) {
        perror("fcntl release lock failed");
    } else {
        printf("Process %d: Lock released successfully.\n", getpid());
    }

    close(fd);
    return 0;
}

Code Mechanism: The program initializes a struct flock structure, setting l_type = F_WRLCK to request an exclusive lock. Using F_SETLKW ensures the call blocks if another process holds a conflicting lock. After completing file I/O operations, l_type is reassigned to F_UNLCK to release control.

Distributed Mutual Exclusion Algorithms: Ricart-Agrawala vs. Token Ring

In distributed systems without shared memory or a central global clock, achieving Mutual Exclusion across independent nodes requires specialized algorithms. Distributed mutual exclusion algorithms ensure that at most one node accesses a shared critical section (CS) at any instant. Two prominent distributed mutual exclusion algorithms are the permission-based Ricart-Agrawala Algorithm and the token-based Token Ring Algorithm.

1. Algorithmic Principles

  • Ricart-Agrawala Algorithm (Permission-Based): Utilizes logical timestamps (Lamport's Logical Clocks). When a node \(N_i\) wants to enter the critical section, it generates a request message with timestamp \(T_i\) and node ID \(i\), broadcasting REQUEST(T_i, i) to all \(N-1\) other nodes. Nodes receiving the request immediately send a REPLY unless they are currently in the CS or also requesting the CS with a lower timestamp (higher priority), in which case the REPLY is deferred. Node \(N_i\) enters the CS only after receiving REPLY messages from all \(N-1\) nodes.
  • Token Ring Algorithm (Token-Based): Arranges all \(N\) network nodes in a logical ring topology (\(N_0 \rightarrow N_1 \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow N_{N-1} \rightarrow N_0\)). A single unique control packet called the Token circulates around the ring. A node holding the token is granted permission to enter the CS. Upon exiting the CS (or if it does not require CS access), the node passes the token to its immediate downstream neighbor in the ring.
graph LR N0((Node 0)) -->|Token Pass| N1((Node 1)) N1 -->|Token Pass| N2((Node 2)) N2 -->|Token Pass| N3((Node 3)) N3 -->|Token Pass| N0

2. Detailed Comparison & Message Complexity

Metric / Attribute Ricart-Agrawala Algorithm Token Ring Algorithm
Message Complexity (Per CS Entry) \(2(N - 1)\) messages (\(N - 1\) requests + \(N - 1\) replies). \(0\) to \(N - 1\) messages (Average \(N / 2\) when idle, 1 message when passing token).
Synchronization Delay \(T\) (One message propagation delay). \(0\) to \((N - 1)T\) (Depends on token position in the ring).
Node Failure Impact High. If any node crashes, requests block indefinitely unless fault-tolerant timeout mechanisms exist. Token loss or node failure breaks the ring. Requires ring re-configuration and election protocols to regenerate token.
Network Overhead Heavy burst messages during request phases. Zero overhead when idle. Continuous background message traffic as token circulates endlessly even when no node needs CS.
State Information Required Each node must know identities of all other \(N-1\) nodes in the system. Each node only needs to know the address of its immediate successor in the ring.

Performance Synthesis: The Ricart-Agrawala algorithm minimizes synchronization delay to a single message transmission time \(T\), but incurs high message complexity \(2(N-1)\) per CS invocation. The Token Ring algorithm avoids broadcast overhead and prevents starvation naturally through ring ordering, but incurs constant baseline network traffic circulating the token even during idle periods.

Android and iOS Mobile Operating System Architectures & Power Management

Mobile operating systems operate under stringent hardware constraints, including limited battery energy capacity, restricted physical RAM, thermal limits, and real-time responsiveness expectations. Modern mobile architectures (Android and iOS) adopt highly structured, layered system models to balance performance, security, and energy efficiency.

1. Architectural Layer Comparison

graph TB subgraph Android Stack A1[System Apps] --> A2[Java API Framework] A2 --> A3[ART Runtime & Native Libraries] A3 --> A4[Hardware Abstraction Layer HAL] A4 --> A5[Linux Kernel] end subgraph iOS Stack I1[Cocoa Touch Layer SwiftUI / UIKit] --> I2[Media Layer Core Graphics / Metal] I2 --> I3[Core Services SQLite / GCD] I3 --> I4[Core OS / Mach-BSD Hybrid Kernel XNU] end
  • Android Architecture: Built on top of a customized Linux Kernel providing driver management, process isolation, and power management. Above the kernel sits the Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) exposing standard interfaces to hardware. The Android Runtime (ART) executes Dalvik bytecode using Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) and Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation. High-level applications run on top of the Java/Kotlin API Framework.
  • iOS Architecture: Built on the XNU Kernel (a Mach microkernel and BSD hybrid within the Darwin OS foundation). The architecture comprises four layers: Core OS (low-level networking, security), Core Services (Grand Central Dispatch, SQLite), Media Layer (Metal, Core Audio), and Cocoa Touch (UIKit, SwiftUI for touch interfaces).

2. Power Management & Background Process Suspension

To maximize battery longevity, mobile operating systems restrict background process execution and aggressively suspend idle applications.

Power Management Feature Android Power Subsystem iOS Power Subsystem
CPU Frequency Scaling DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling) via Linux CPUfreq governors. Utilizes ARM big.LITTLE core allocation. Integrated low-power CPU efficiency cores dynamically scheduled via Mach kernel scheduler.
Background Process Suspension Doze Mode & App Standby Buckets: Batches background execution into maintenance windows when device is stationary. Groups apps into buckets (Active, Working Set, Frequent, Rare). Strict App Lifecycle: Active \(\rightarrow\) Inactive \(\rightarrow\) Background \(\rightarrow\) Suspended. Suspended apps remain frozen in RAM with zero CPU usage.
Background Task APIs WorkManager and JobScheduler for deferred execution. Wakelocks (PowerManager.WakeLock) explicitly keep CPU awake. BGTaskScheduler for scheduled background tasks and push-notification-triggered updates.
Memory Reclamation Low Memory Killer (LMK) driver terminates processes based on oom_adj scores when RAM runs low. Jetsam daemon terminates suspended background applications aggressively when free memory drops below threshold.

Key Insight: iOS enforces zero background CPU usage for suspended apps by freezing process threads in RAM, freeing memory via Jetsam when necessary. Android uses Doze Mode and App Standby Buckets to throttle network access and defer job execution to periodic maintenance windows, mitigating battery drain caused by background services.

Kernel Memory Allocation: Buddy System vs. Slab Allocator

Kernel memory allocation differs significantly from standard user-space dynamic allocation. The operating system kernel requires allocation routines that are fast, deterministic, minimize internal and external fragmentation, and can allocate physically contiguous pages required for Direct Memory Access (DMA) hardware devices.

1. Architectural Comparison

  • Buddy System Allocator: Allocates memory from a large contiguous power-of-two block (\(2^L\)). When a request of size \(S\) is received, it is rounded up to the smallest power of two \(2^k \ge S\). If a block of size \(2^k\) is not available, a larger block \(2^{k+1}\) is split into two equal-sized "buddies". Reclaiming memory is extremely fast because when a block is freed, the allocator checks if its adjacent buddy is also free, merging them back into a single \(2^{k+1}\) block.
    Limitation: Causes high internal fragmentation when request sizes do not align closely with powers of two.
  • Slab Allocator: Operates on top of the Buddy System to handle small kernel data structures (e.g., task_struct, inode, file). Memory is partitioned into Caches, each dedicated to a specific type of kernel object. Caches consist of one or more Slabs (contiguous physical pages allocated via the Buddy System). Slabs exist in three states: Full, Partial, or Empty.
    Advantage: Eliminates internal fragmentation for kernel objects and eliminates initialization overhead by retaining pre-allocated, pre-constructed object instances.

2. Step-by-Step Trace of Buddy System Allocation

Consider an initial total physical block of 1 MB (\(1024\text{ KB}\)) spanning address range [0 to 1024 KB]. We execute three sequential allocation requests: Req 1 = 100 KB, Req 2 = 240 KB, and Req 3 = 60 KB.

Step-by-Step Execution Trace:

  1. Initial Block: One single block of \(1024\text{ KB}\) at [0 - 1024 KB].
  2. Request 1 (100 KB):
    Required power-of-two size: \(2^{\lceil \log_2 100 \rceil} = 128\text{ KB}\).
    • Split \(1024\text{ KB}\) block into two \(512\text{ KB}\) buddies: [0-512 KB] and [512-1024 KB].
    • Split [0-512 KB] into two \(256\text{ KB}\) buddies: [0-256 KB] and [256-512 KB].
    • Split [0-256 KB] into two \(128\text{ KB}\) buddies: [0-128 KB] and [128-256 KB].
    • Allocate [0 - 128 KB] to Req 1 (100 KB).
    • Internal Fragmentation for Req 1: \(128\text{ KB} - 100\text{ KB} = 28\text{ KB}\).
  3. Request 2 (240 KB):
    Required power-of-two size: \(2^{\lceil \log_2 240 \rceil} = 256\text{ KB}\).
    • An exact free block of \(256\text{ KB}\) exists at [256 - 512 KB].
    • Allocate [256 - 512 KB] to Req 2 (240 KB).
    • Internal Fragmentation for Req 2: \(256\text{ KB} - 240\text{ KB} = 16\text{ KB}\).
  4. Request 3 (60 KB):
    Required power-of-two size: \(2^{\lceil \log_2 60 \rceil} = 64\text{ KB}\).
    • Smallest available free block larger than \(64\text{ KB}\) is the \(128\text{ KB}\) block at [128 - 256 KB].
    • Split [128-256 KB] into two \(64\text{ KB}\) buddies: [128-192 KB] and [192-256 KB].
    • Allocate [128 - 192 KB] to Req 3 (60 KB).
    • Internal Fragmentation for Req 3: \(64\text{ KB} - 60\text{ KB} = 4\text{ KB}\).
